1#א: Well washed. Shach wrote this is not to say that stam we establish regarding anything cooked in it that there was clinging fat, as Rosh and Taz wrote in seif 3 regarding rinsing — that even if it is not ben yomo we establish on it clinging fat and that it was not well scraped, for only regarding rinsing do we say stam there is clinging fat on them because now he is rinsing them; but when it was cooked in a pot we say stam there was no clinging fat on them. And what Mechaber wrote "well washed" is to exclude when it is known clearly that it was not well washed.
1#ב: Taste. Explanation: the meat imparts taste to the bowl and the bowl to the fish and still all is heter. And Taz wrote and these are his words: (and all this is in Bach; but regarding prohibition, even many times noten taam bar noten taam is forbidden, for there the concept of noten taam bar noten taam of heter does not apply). One may learn from this that there is no danger in eating fish that has taste of meat from what was cooked in a ben yomo meat vessel, for they said in the Gemara that many ate fish that came up in a bowl, etc.; and see siman 116 what he wrote there until here is his language.
2#א: Egg. Shach wrote: even if it is peeled, if the pot is well washed.
2#ב: In its shell. Rashba wrote that the egg shell is clearly perforated, and when a person cooks it he finds the egg itself colored from that color; therefore the Sages forbade an egg of a chick and permitted a forbidden egg, for that one emits broth of a chick and this one emits only mere broth, end of his words. And Taz wrote and requires study from what Rama wrote in siman 86 seif 5 that if the egg is pierced its law is like peeled, for every egg shell is perforated — so why distinguish a hole that developed or did not develop — and he left it requiring study. (And it appears to me that this is certainly if the egg was cooked all day — we see it does not emit at all but rather certainly hardens moment by moment until because of this those fine holes closed; therefore regarding an egg of impure fowl it does not forbid until it is pierced with a large hole; but here if it was cooked with meat then it absorbs well through those holes with difficulty, and therefore it is forbidden to eat it with kutach. Proof for this from Rashba himself who wrote in siman 66: if blood is found in an egg that one placed on hot coals to constrict — it is plain that the dish is not forbidden since there was no sauce — it forbids only the measure of a peel, and the egg shell is no less than the measure of a peel; and here he wrote that the egg shell is perforated — but certainly it does not emit anything through those small holes, investigate.)
2#ג: To forbid. L'chatchila to eat it with kutach; but b'dieved if he placed it in kutach it is permitted; but to cook them l'chatchila in a meat pot in order to eat them with kutach is forbidden even for Mechaber.
2#ד: In a vessel. Shach wrote: it appears that even to place them by way of pouring is permitted, but it is difficult, for he wrote in seif 3 that if one pours from a kli rishon of meat onto a dairy vessel its law is like a kli rishon and it forbids if it was ben yomo; and one must say that here he deals only with permitting to place them without pouring. Nevertheless regarding the halachah requires study, for it appears that if one pours from a meat vessel onto a dairy vessel it is permitted since it is b'dieved; and some say regarding what we forbid meat bowls that were rinsed in a dairy cauldron — there it is different as Ran wrote: who will tell us that emission of meat and emission of milk will not mix in themselves without the intermediary of water — therefore it is not noten taam bar noten taam; therefore it appears regarding fish that were cooked, etc. And further, what we permit as noten taam bar noten taam is not because they hold the first taste does not spread until the third — for if so, in other prohibitions too we would say so for one who does not hold chein nafsho, and we permit only in basar b'chalav and the like where there are two tastes of heter; therefore specifically when the second taste stood in heter without mixture of milk do we say so; but here where the second taste did not stand by itself at all but as soon as it came into existence it mixed with the taste of milk — it is reasonable and certain that it is forbidden, as Semak wrote, end of his words. And all this does not apply to pouring; and so is the view of Issur VeHeter that if one pours from a kli rishon of meat onto one of milk it is permitted; and even the Rav in Turei Chayim there din 12 wrote that all his words appear to me to be the halachah since they are matters of taste; but it appears to me they did not practice to be lenient in such a case; however in great loss or time of need one may rely on him. And also in responsum of Masat Binyamin siman 2 he ruled so and wrote that all who are stringent in this are only among those who wonder, see there; and see s.k. 17.
2#ה: Sharp. The sharpness of spices makes it as if it is visible, and specifically the food itself that is sharp is made for improvement; but it does not make the pot for improvement; and see above siman 96 and siman 103 seif 6.
2#ו: The absorbed. Explanation: we do not say regarding spices that since they are made for taste they are not nullified, since their prohibition is not because of themselves; and see above siman 98 seif 8. And Taz wrote: if the absorbed amount is unknown, one needs sixty against all the spices.
3#א: Permitted. Shach wrote: this is b'dieved; but l'chatchila one should not rinse them even for Mechaber, as Mechaber wrote in Orach Chaim siman 452.
3#ב: Fat. Explanation: even if there was only clinging fat on one of them, all is forbidden, because the second taste immediately imparts taste into the substance and it is not a second noten taam in heter; and also the fat touches the second vessel and the vessel becomes forbidden and again all becomes forbidden. And accordingly, even if one of them is not ben yomo and the clinging fat is on the one that is not ben yomo, all is forbidden; but if the clinging fat is on the one that is ben yomo, that one which is ben yomo is permitted and the one that is not ben yomo is forbidden, end of his words Shach.
3#ג: They forbid. For who will tell us that emission of meat and emission of milk will not mix in themselves without the intermediary of water — Ran. And Taz wrote: and nevertheless, if water or vegetables were cooked in a dairy ben yomo pot and one stuck into it a ben yomo meat spoon and there is not sixty against the spoon, they forbid one another even if both were well scraped; and he also wrote what Rama wrote: all the vessels are permitted — this is because the one that is ben yomo is permitted since it receives spoilage; and the one that is not ben yomo is also not forbidden from the one that is ben yomo, for it is noten taam bar noten taam, and it is still heter after it entered this vessel since it is not ben yomo there is no prohibition on it. And even though Rama wrote in siman 94 seif 5 to forbid the vessel that is not ben yomo as a stringency, it appears that specifically there he holds one should be stringent because of marit ayin since one pours food into a vessel that is as if it were ben yomo — therefore one forbids the vessel that is not ben yomo, and this does not apply here, end of his words. And Shach wrote in name of Issur VeHeter that there is no difference whether one rinsed bowls with bowls or spoons with spoons or ladles with ladles, and we do not say that what is used in a kli sheni does not forbid, end of his words. And it appears to me that specifically from stam we are concerned lest he used a spoon or ladle in a kli rishon, as we are concerned in such a case regarding hagalah of vessels; but if it is clear to him that he did not use a spoon or ladle, only a kli sheni within twenty-four hours, certainly it does not forbid b'dieved, and so is practiced (and Peri Chadash wrote on this and the law is not correct, but anything used while yad soledes bo applied within twenty-four hours is forbidden).
3#ד: L'chatchila. Since it is not food but mere water, it is like l'chatchila and we forbid it since it absorbed from spoiled prohibition.
3#ה: Together. Shach wrote and it teaches us: some say that if one rinsed meat bowls in the dairy cauldron itself all is forbidden; rather, even if one rinsed a meat vessel and a dairy vessel together in one vessel, all is forbidden, for the water in the kli rishon emits and absorbs and becomes nevelah.
3#ו: Second. Taz wrote: even if they were soiled, as he wrote afterward regarding pouring; and all the more so pouring is stricter than kli sheni for us. And Maharshal disagrees on this and wrote that if there was grime from meat and milk it forbids even in a kli sheni, for there is concern the grime will dissolve in the water and be considered as the substance of the prohibition; however since this is somewhat a stringency, the teacher need not ask about this if they were soiled until it becomes clear to him automatically; but regarding pouring one must ask if the rinsing was by way of pouring, since stam they are accustomed to pour on them from a kli rishon by the fire — if it is not known to him that it was not by pouring, then one need not ask if there was food remnant, end of his words. And it appears to me for practical halachah to decide that regarding pouring one must forbid both if there were food remnants from both; and if one is soiled and the second clean, then the clean one becomes forbidden; but in a kli sheni food remnants do not forbid, for we establish that even yad soledes bo in a kli sheni does not absorb and does not emit.
3#ז: Its law. Taz wrote: one may challenge — behold it is noten taam bar noten taam; and it appears that since we forbid above as those who forbid whom Rama brought in this seif, because it is like taste of meat and milk mixed together — that is, since the two tastes mix in one vessel and chein nafsho — it is comparable to our considering the splash of pouring as if it were in the vessel from which he pours; therefore he forbids the vessel onto which he pours since it too is ben yomo; but if this vessel onto which he pours is not ben yomo, it is not forbidden, for it is no worse than that which he wrote nearby that the vessels are permitted if one is not ben yomo.
3#ח: They will absorb. Shach wrote: and even though in siman 68 seif 6 it appears from Rama's words that pouring cooks kedei kelipah — one must say that although it cooks so that poultry emits and absorbs, nevertheless a hard vessel does not absorb, for it does not emit and absorb at once like a hard vessel; however regarding the halachah it appears as Hagahot ShaDa wrote that they are forbidden, since we establish that pouring cooks, as will be explained in siman 105; if so it is considered actual cooking and absorbs even in a vessel; however all this is when clinging fat is on them, but if they are clean certainly there is room to permit because of noten taam bar noten taam; but where it is a vessel of prohibition where noten taam bar noten taam does not apply, it appears that even if clean it is forbidden, and requires study in this, for perhaps even cooking does not cook so much that it emits from the vessel and absorbs into the vessel; and accordingly also in meat and milk vessels where one is clean and one not clean — the clean is forbidden and the not clean requires study whether we say that since the clean is nat bar lichtmile it returns and forbids the second each time he pours onto it, or we say pouring does not cook so much and one should be stringent with both where there is no great loss.
3#ט: Were rinsed. In Issur VeHeter it is written: even if they are accustomed in that house to rinse in a kli rishon they are permitted through a double doubt — a doubt lest they were not rinsed with them, and if you say they were rinsed, a doubt lest it was not ben yomo.
4#_: Ash. Shach wrote: this law requires study, for it is not found in any posek, and he brings proof from poskim that proves the opposite, see there. And Taz wrote: according to this law there is no prohibition if lye called zeif made from milk fell into the dish, for the lye has ash when they make it from milk, and requires study; for in siman 87 Rama wrote that the vessel in which they make water for head-washing is accustomed to mix meat and milk there, end of his words; and since nat bar lichtmile there is no basar b'chalav prohibition at all. And I also found in Rashal's words: and I found in Maharil's words that once a child came and said a piece of lye made from milk fell into the pot, and he said one should not believe the child — it appears that if it certainly fell, the lye forbids; and behold it is nat bar lichtmile, and requires study for practical halachah (and Nachalat Binyamin wrote one may distinguish that here he speaks only of reducing clinging fat on the surface of the vessel through ash, unlike in the substance of the milk, see there).
5#_: Salt. The reason: in salt, kutach that falls on it is visible and is not nullified, and we are concerned lest one salt meat in it; but in vinegar the prohibition is not visible and it is nullified in sixty.
6#א: Chest. For they are careful that nothing falls from one to the other, unlike in seif 5 where it does not occur to him that kutach might fall into the salt.
6#ב: L'chatchila. This is specifically when uncovered, as in seif 5.
7#_: In milk. The reason is in Shach: salt has no power to emit taste from a vessel; and accordingly, even in a forbidden bowl it is permitted. And Rashal wrote: nevertheless I praise the Ashkenaz custom of having vessels made for salt, one for meat and one for milk, for sometimes during the meal one's hands are soiled from meat and he takes salt there and afterward will take for milk, and likewise the reverse, end of his words.
